content:
Glenmorangie is joining the wave of ultra-aged whiskey releases. On Thursday, the Highland distillery announced the launch of a 50-year-old single malt, marking the distillery’s oldest Scotch yet.

The half century-old whisky is one of the final Glenmorangie expressions to come from barley malted on site, a process that the distillery ceased in 1977. The special release is the result of the vision of Glenmorangie’s director of distilling Dr. Bill Lumsden, who oversaw the Scotch’s maturation for its last 30 years. After joining the team in 1995, Lumsden identified a number of casks with potential for long term aging. In 1999, Lumsden brought together a small selection of bourbon cask- and sherry butt-aged whiskies for the project, and left the marriage to rest in a hogshead barrel for another 27 years.

Glenmorangie 50 Years Old was non-chill filtered and bottled at 45.7 percent ABV (91.4 proof). Brand tasting notes highlight baking spices, toffee, and leather on the nose. The palate brings pepper, tea leaves, grape must, and oak tannin, leading into a long, spice-forward finish.

The distillery commissioned renowned ceramicists Peter and Laurie Pincus to create the sleek porcelain package design. The pair developed an elegant, oval-shaped vessel that features 50 different colors as a nod to the whisky’s age.

The exceedingly exclusive bottling — only 149 numbered bottles of Glenmorangie 50 Years Old exist — hit the market for a suggested retail price of £25,800 ($36,000). It is available to select retailers, through Moët Hennessy Private Client Team network, and at the distillery’s visitor center in Tain, Scotland.

content:
Chardonnay is one of the world’s most popular grape varieties, but not every bottle is created equally. With the grape’s wide range of expressions and price points, it can sometimes seem difficult to find the middle ground between the ultra-rich, overly oaky budget bottles and the more nuanced, terroir-driven wines with daunting price tags.

But you don’t have to spend a fortune to explore all that Chardonnay has to offer beyond the notorious butter bombs that once gave the grape a bad name. To help pinpoint which bottles deliver the ample quality without the sticker shock that can come with high-end Chardonnay, we asked nine sommeliers from across the country which bottles they think offer the most bang for your buck. From surprisingly affordable White Burgundy to complex Chardonnays from buzzy Oregon producers, here are their picks for the best value Chardonnays.

The best bang-for-your-buck Chardonnays, according to sommeliers:

  • Lioco Sonoma Coast Chardonnay
  • On Wine Hill “Millerandage” Chardonnay 2024
  • Brij Wines Chardonnay
  • Enfield Wine Co. Citrine Chardonnay
  • Enfield Wine Co. Brosseau Chardonnay
  • Evening Land Vineyards Seven Springs Chardonnay
  • Lingua Franca Avni Chardonnay 2024
  • Scar of the Sea SLO Coast Chardonnay 2024
  • Domaine des Terres de Chatenay Mâcon-Villages “La Cuvée de Béracius” 2025

“I’m quite fond of the Lioco Sonoma Coast Chardonnay. It’s an unoaked style that tends to show bright acidity and some Chablis-like qualities. Generally, you can get it for around $25 retail, and it’s from a small, family-run winery.” —Gregory Wilson, sommelier, Beckon, Denver

“When it comes to delicious and affordable Chardonnay, so much great wine is being made on the West Coast right now. One of my favorites that has caught my attention lately is the On Wine Hill “Millerandage” Chardonnay 2024 from the Willamette Valley, Ore. Jeff Vejr is doing some really cool things in Oregon, and for this particular wine, he is using a specific clone (548) of Chardonnay that is predisposed to what is known as ‘millerandage’ or ‘hens and chicks.’ This causes uneven ripening of the grape clusters so some berries will be larger while others remain small. This increases the skin-to-juice ratio, giving the wine a beautiful, finely grained texture, as well as a natural kick of acidity from the tart, smaller berries in the bunch. This wine has the textural richness to hold up to a variety of foods, but it’s also fresh and fun enough to be enjoyed on its own!” —Cameron Dellinger, wine director, Jungsik, New York City

“I would love to shout out the Chardonnay from Brij Wines from the San Luis Obispo Coast. This project, from renowned California winemaker and master sommelier Raj Parr, uses fruit purchased from local growers who share his passion for sustainable farming. The winemaking is as thoughtful and non-interventionist as you find in any of the bottlings at Parr Wines but at a fraction of the price, typically retailing around $35. The wine itself has the rich texture and subtle oak aromas that I’m looking for in a California Chardonnay, but with salinity and freshness that speak to the wine’s coastal origins.” —Audrey Dowling, beverage director, Rye Bunny, Washington, D.C.

“I’ve always had a soft spot in my heart for the wines of Enfield Wine Company and found they’ve always delivered far beyond its price point. Winemaker John Lockwood comes from the pedigree of Littorai and Failla, two wineries that I would define as American winemaking excellence, as well as a commitment to working with small farmers in select California heritage sites that stand out to him. At $30 retail, the Citrine is far from the traditional California Chardonnay that has left a bad taste in the mouth of many wine drinkers, but offers a soft touch of yellow apple and citrus with a round tropical finish bursting with a kiss of saline minerality. Just writing about the wine makes me want to open another bottle from Enfield sooner than later.” —Angel Prado, lead sommelier, Sorelle, Charleston

“I love the Enfield Wine Co. Brosseau Chardonnay. It’s planted on super high elevation, limestone soils in Chalone, giving it this really distinct California terroir. There’s lean, mineral, acidity but it finishes lush, savory, round, and complex. It’s a great wine to get you from start to finish in the meal. The winemakers are really excited to be sharing the unique terroirs of California while celebrating dedicated farmers and growers in the region.” —Charlotte Mirzoeff, general manager and beverage director, Arthur, Brooklyn

“I think Evening Land Vineyards Chardonnay ‘Seven Springs’ from Eola Amity Hills, Ore. is the best affordable Chardonnay. At around $29 retail, this wine is as close to Meursault as you can find in the U.S. and at a fraction of the cost. It’s slightly reductive, just ripe enough and loaded with the savory mineral notes that are the backbone of all great Chardonnays.” —Francesco Grosso, wine director, Ai Fiori, NYC

“The current belief that the best place outside Burgundy to grow Chardonnay is the Willamette Valley, Ore. I have consistently been pleased with the Burgundian character of Chardonnays from Willamette Valley. My favorite is Lingua Franca Avni Chardonnay 2024, made by cherished Burgundy winemaker Dominique Lafon and Master Sommelier Larry Stone, with protégé Thomas Savre. It tastes like dipping your toe in a Meursault.” —Lindsey Geddes, wine director, Carversteak, Las Vegas

“With Scar of the Sea SLO Coast Chardonnay, you’re getting a bright and fresh expression of coastal California Chardonnay, with a long élevage and incredible farming practices. It has energy and depth, and punches way above its price point!” —Shanna Nasiri, owner, With Others, Brooklyn

“Domaine des Terres de Chatenay Mâcon-Villages ‘La Cuvée de Béracius’ 2025. I’m always excited to find a White Burgundy that overdelivers, and this old-vine Mâcon-Villages from Jean-Claude and Marie-Odile Janin is one I keep coming back to. Made from 70-year-old Chardonnay vines planted in the clay-limestone soils of Péronne, it has vibrant fruit, chalky minerality, and incredible tension. It has the focus and depth I love in great Burgundy while still feeling fresh and distinctive, so much so that we carry it at Le Pavillon. This limited-production cuvée is that rarest of finds: a true ‘unicorn’ wine from the Mâconnais.” —John Osborne, head sommelier, Le Pavillon, NYC

content:
This article is part of our Cocktail Chatter series, where we dive into the wild, weird, and wondrous corners of history to share over a cocktail and impress your friends.

The French baguette is losing steam: From 1970 to 2022, the number of traditional boulangeries in France dropped by roughly 400 a year from about 55,000 to 35,000. In response, the United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization (UNESCO) granted the French baguette its Intangible Cultural Heritage designation to preserve the tradition of breadmaking.

Though the numbers might suggest this culinary staple is waning, there still appears to be no shortage of baguettes in the country. In Paris, pedestrians will see locals and tourists alike walking the streets with the loaf of bread in tow, either clutched under the arm or poking out of a bag. The city also hosts a prestigious annual competition to find the best baguette in Paris, in which over 100 bakers submit their best loaves to be measured, weighed, and tasted for a chance to win a cash prize and a one-year contract to be the exclusive baguette supplier to the French president’s residence. But for those looking to experience the country’s carb culture in the most authentic way, there’s only one type of baguette to order.

The best baguettes slung around Paris are of a certain, government-controlled variety, thanks to a French law passed in 1993. The 1993 décret du pain (the bread decree), which sought to protect the sacred practice of breadmaking, legislated that baguettes labeled “tradition” must be made with just wheat flour, water, salt, and yeast or sourdough starter — no preservatives or other additives. The dough can also never be frozen, and the baguettes must be baked on the site where they are sold. “Baguettes de tradition” is the only government-controlled bread category.

The designation works much like the Appellation d’Origine Contrôlée (AOC) system, which mandates that wines labeled under a given region must follow specific quality and production standards, such as permitting certain grapes, aging methods, and additives. Similarly, at boulangeries around the country, loaves of bread are often placed into different baskets, with each label corresponding to the respective variety.

Ordering a stick from the tradition — aptly named and easy to remember, as it is the most traditional variety — basket ensures you’ll be eating the highest-quality bread, one with a craggly and sturdy exterior that opens to a bouncy, stretchy interior. Flavors of toasted and fresh yeast will be strong throughout.

Other baguette varieties include the “baguette classique” (also labeled as “ordinaire”) and the “baguette aux céréales” (also labeled as “aux graines”). A classique is a run-of-the-mill baguette, not protected under any government regulations, meaning the dough could have been frozen or it could contain preservatives to elongate its shelf life. A baguette aux céréales is the multigrain version of a baguette, with seeds and grains studding the loaf.

When ordering a baguette — whether de tradition or not — there are some other ways to communicate with the boulanger to ensure the bread will suit your specifications. Those who like sturdy, crunchy bread can ask for one bien cuite, or well cooked. Those who like a softer and more chewy loaf can ask for one pas trop cuite, or not too cooked. In either case, the baker will inspect their loaves and hand you the one that best suits your needs.

Whether mass-produced or not, any baguette in France is likely to be tasty and to evoke warm, happy feelings of European life. But when traveling the country, ordering your bread à la française can elevate that feeling, one yeasty crunch at a time.

content:
Dating back to the late-1800s, the Manhattan is widely considered the first “modern” cocktail. It’s an incredibly simple formula of whiskey, sweet vermouth, and a couple dashes of bitters, and if you stick to the script, the only room for customization comes from choosing between spicy rye and rich bourbon.

While the cocktail is relatively straightforward, its effortless balance gave way to numerous variations. It also inspired a new category of cocktails made by mixing spirits with fortified wine that have become classics in their own right like the Rob Roy or Vieux Carré.

Since bartenders have been riffing on this cocktail for over a century, we tapped a few to see how they put their own twist on the Manhattan when making the drink at home. From swapping vermouth for a rich amaro to sneaking in other spirits like mezcal, here’s how nine top bartenders make Manhattans at home.

Kyle Jackson

Bar director, Markette and The Argyle, New York City

For a Manhattan at home, I don’t think there’s much reason to reinvent it. The drink is iconic because of its simplicity, so for me, it comes down to choosing ingredients that each bring something specific. I use Michter’s rye because it has the spice and complexity I want from a rye, but also a lingering finish that carries through the vermouth instead of disappearing underneath it. For the sweet vermouth, I go with Noilly Prat Rouge. French sweet vermouth might be a slightly controversial choice for a Manhattan, but I prefer the finesse of Noilly Prat here. It gives the drink enough richness and herbal character without becoming too assertive. My spec is also very easy to remember: 2:1:2, which conveniently happens to be Manhattan’s original area code.

Ingredients

  • 2 ounces Michter’s Rye Whiskey
  • 1 ounce Noilly Prat Rouge sweet vermouth
  • 2 dashes Angostura bitters
  • Garnish: cherry and orange oil

Directions

  1. Add all ingredients to a mixing glass with ice. Stir to combine.
  2. Strain into a chilled Martini glass. Garnish with a cherry, then express an orange peel over the surface of the drink and discard the peel.

Owen Gibler

Partner and beverage director, Bar Roza, Nashville

When making drinks at home, avoiding pitfalls creates a more measurable change than aiming for exotic tweaks. Pitfall one: vermouth. Every article mentioning a vermouth cocktail should include a disclaimer noting that it is a fortified wine and oxidizes quickly. The trick is to make lots of Manhattans and never have a bottle open for more than a week. Pitfall two: ice. Home ice is generally smaller and melts faster than a cocktail bar’s ice, so use less ice and a shorter stir. And pitfall three: warm glassware. Stick your coupe into the freezer for a few minutes before using it. It’s such an easy move that creates a dramatic improvement.

Ingredients

  • 2 ¼ ounces Woody Creek Rye
  • ¾ ounce Cocchi Vermouth di Torino
  • 2 dashes Angostura bitters
  • Garnish: cherry

Directions

  1. Add all ingredients into a mixing glass with ice. Stir to combine.
  2. Strain into a chilled coupe and garnish with a cherry.

James Grant

Beverage director, Fairmont Royal York, Montreal, Canada

I love a Manhattan. More specifically, I love experimenting with a Manhattan. The classic specification of two parts whiskey to one part sweet vermouth finished with a couple of dashes of bitters is certainly serviceable, but the simple formula can sometimes feel a little bare-bones or thin. I typically gravitate toward cocktails such as a Black Manhattan, À La Louisiane, Bobby Burns, or Tipperary, which introduce an added layer of complexity through the inclusion of a liqueur. With that in mind, when I make a Manhattan at home, I tend to dress it up slightly with the addition of an amaro. I choose one that complements both the herbal profile of the vermouth and the character of the whiskey. That touch of sweetness also provides a little extra body, helping to keep the cocktail from feeling too lean.

Ingredients

  • 2 ounces Lot No. 40 Rye Whisky
  • 1 ounce Cocchi Storico Vermouth di Torino
  • ¼ ounce Amaro Meletti
  • 2 dashes Angostura bitters
  • 2 dashes orange bitters
  • Garnish: brandied cherry and orange oil

Directions

  1. Add all ingredients to a mixing glass with ice. Stir to combine.
  2. Strain into a chilled Nick & Nora glass. Garnish with a brandied cherry, then express an orange peel over the surface of the drink and discard the peel.

Johnisha Williams

Bar manager, Commander’s Palace, New Orleans

I like a perfect Manhattan because using both sweet and dry vermouth gives the drink a nice balance while still letting the rye shine. I also like using both Angostura and Peychaud’s as a little nod to New Orleans and how we make our Sazerac here at Commander’s. The Angostura gives it that familiar spice, while the Peychaud’s adds a lighter, floral note. I also really enjoy rye as an introduction to the whiskey world. I personally don’t typically reach for bourbon, and I find rye to be a little easier and more approachable for someone who doesn’t normally drink whiskey. It still has that depth and character you expect from whiskey, but I find the spice and overall profile makes it an enjoyable starting point. For me, a Manhattan is a great way to introduce someone to rye without asking them to drink it neat or on the rocks.

Ingredients

  • 2 ounces rye whiskey
  • ½ ounce sweet vermouth
  • ½ ounce dry vermouth
  • 2 dashes Angostura bitters
  • 1 dash Peychaud’s bitters
  • Garnish: lemon twist

Directions

  1. Add all ingredients into a mixing glass with ice. Stir to combine.
  2. Strain into a child coupe or Nick and Nora glass. Garnish with a lemon twist.

Chuck Worley

Bar manager, Lowland, Charleston

This vision was born out of my love for mezcal. I love a split base, booze-forward cocktail, so I’m using equal parts mezcal and a sweeter rye, pulling back the sweet vermouth just a touch, throwing in a couple dashes of classic bitters and a small bar spoon of Luxardo cherry juice.

Ingredients

  • 1 ¼ ounces Banhez mezcal
  • 1 ¼ ounces Angel’s Envy Rye
  • ½ ounce Carpano Antica Formula
  • 4 dashes Angostura bitters
  • 1 bar spoon of Luxardo cherry syrup
  • Ganish: Luxardo cherry and orange oil

Directions

  1. Add all ingredients to a mixing glass with ice. Stir to combine.
  2. Strain into a chilled coupe glass. Garnish with a Luxardo cherry, then express an orange peel over the surface of the drink and discard the peel.

Kristine Nguyen

Head bartender, Bludorn, Houston

This is a riff on a Black Manhattan with pandan adding a subtle tropical note and amaro bringing enough bitterness to keep the drink grounded. I’ve always enjoyed Black Manhattans because they give you so much room to play with the level and style of bitterness. This recipe is meant to do the same.

Ingredients

  • 1 ½ ounces Tres Tribus Mezcal
  • ¾ ounce Foro Amaro
  • ½ ounce sweet vermouth
  • 1 bar spoon Kota pandan liqueur
  • Garnish: lemon twist

Directions

  1. Add all ingredients to a mixing glass with ice. Stir to combine.
  2. Strain into a coupe or your preferred glass. Garnish with lemon twist.

Austin Krudys

Beverage manager, The Chloe, Nashville

My go-to Manhattan is a Black Manhattan, a simple twist on the classic recipe that swaps out sweet vermouth for Averna amaro. The Averna introduces a unique layer of complexity, leaning a bit more bitter and herbaceous. As a bonus for home bartenders, Averna doesn’t require refrigeration like sweet vermouth does, giving it a much longer shelf life.

Ingredients

  • 2 ounces high-proof rye like Rittenhouse Rye
  • 1 ounce Averna amaro
  • 2 dashes Regan’s orange bitters
  • Garnish: Luxardo cherry

Directions

  1. Add all ingredients to a mixing glass with ice. Stir to combine.
  2. Strain into a chilled Nick & Nora glass. Garnish with a Luxardo cherry.

Oscar Valle

Co-founder, TONANA, San Miguel de Allende, Mexico

My go-to at home is a 50/50 Manhattan with Angostura bitters. I love that ratio because it gives the vermouth as much room to shine as the whiskey. Its herbal notes and sweetness balance the spice of the rye, while the Angostura brings everything together. The orange twist adds a bright aroma that lifts the drink. It’s simple to make at home with no special prep. Just remember to keep your vermouth refrigerated after opening so it stays fresh.

Ingredients

  • 1½ ounces rye whiskey
  • 1½ ounces sweet vermouth
  • 2 dashes Angostura bitters
  • Garnish: orange twist

Directions

  1. Add all ingredients to a mixing glass with ice. Stir to combine.
  2. Strain into a chilled coupe or Nick & Nora glass. Express the oils from an orange twist over the drink and use it as the garnish.

Carlo Olcese

Co-owner and director of operations, Bateman’s, NYC

Whenever I make a Manhattan at home, I lean toward the bittersweet twist of a Black Manhattan, replacing sweet vermouth with Averna amaro. The benefit is that I don’t have to worry about stocking fresh vermouth in my fridge every month. I use Angel’s Envy Kentucky Straight Bourbon since its vanilla notes pair incredibly well with the anise flavor of Averna. To finish, I add one dash of Angostura bitters for some baking spice, and about a half spoon of Luxardo cherry syrup to add a touch of sweetness. Once the drink has been poured, I drop a Luxardo cherry at the bottom for a sweet treat at the end of my drink.

Ingredients

  • 2 ounces Angel’s Envy Kentucky Straight Bourbon
  • 1 ounce Averna Amaro
  • 1 dash Angostura bitters
  • ½ bar spoon Luxardo maraschino cherry syrup
  • Garnish: Luxardo cherry

Directions

  1. Add all ingredients to a mixing glass with ice. Stir to combine.
  2. Strain into a chilled, stemmed glass. Garnish with a Luxardo cherry.

content:
This year Oktoberfest began on Saturday, Sept. 19 when the mayor of Munich tapped the first keg of beer. The world’s largest and most famous beer-drinking festival will conclude with a gun salute on the first Sunday of October. Over the festival’s 16 days, the six breweries legally permitted to serve beer anticipate pouring more than 6 million liters of golden, malty lager this year. While it might surprise — or even offend — beer purists, a significant number of those 6 million liters will be diluted with soda.

The traditional combination of beer and lemon soda is called a “radler,” and it’s offered as an option everywhere beer is sold at Oktoberfest. While the official number of beers served is tallied at the end of the fest, the number of radlers sold is not counted. There does not seem to be much national pride for this mixed drink, nonetheless, the radler is an enduring staple of the German festival — there’s even a popular Oktoberfest anthem “Radler Ist Kein Alkohol” poking fun at its ubiquitous nature. Here’s how lemon soda became a fixture of beer’s biggest event.

What is a Radler?

The term “radler” or “radlermass” translates directly to “cyclist” or “cyclist’s liter” in German and its meaning can be traced back to the beverage’s origin story. In 1922, a Bavarian innkeeper named Franz Xaver Kugler was visited by an unexpected group of cyclists stopping for a couple pints before continuing their journey. Either Kugler was running low on beer, or he was concerned for his guests’ safety on the second half of their ride, because he poured them a combination of local beer and lemon-flavored soft drink. As the story goes, he called the mixture a “radler.”

While Kugler is credited as the first to use the term, he was not the first to combine beer with a soft drink. British pubkeepers were pouring beer and lemonade or ginger ale together and calling it “shandy” at least 75 years prior to Kugler debuting the radler. Charles Dickens referenced shandy as an acceptable beverage for an honest man on a hot day in his periodical “All the Year Round” in 1860.

Though not as widely known as the shandy, the radler has also exhibited some serious staying power, and the mixed beverage has only gained in popularity over the last century since Kugler first served one up. While it was once thought of as merely a refreshing beverage for hot summer days, it’s now widely available at all German beer festivals from Starkbierzeit in March to Oktoberfest in early autumn.

Why Drink Radlers?

“I only drink radlers” explains Sally Pilkington, a British expat who’s lived in Munich off and on since 2009 and has been to more than 10 Oktoberfests. “It’s not quite so alcoholic” she adds, “if you’re going to spend four to five hours there and drink a full mass of beer, you’ll get quite drunk.”

Pilkington is referring to the fact that tables in the beer tents at Oktoberfest are reserved for three-plus hour periods. Fest-goers wait in long lines to enter the tents so you’re expected to continue ordering, eating, and drinking once inside. Beer is served in a standard liter mug called a “mass.”

Those looking to practice moderation can purchase a liter of non-alcoholic beer for the same price as normal beer, but radler is the only low-ABV beverage available inside the beer tents. The typical fest beer contains around 6 percent ABV, making a radler around 3 percent ABV.

While an ABV of 6 percent may not seem worrisome, consider the atmosphere inside the tents. Energetic attendees squeeze shoulder to shoulder with friends and strangers in the heat, singing and shouting “prost!” while gulping beer every few seconds. For those looking to pace themselves over the marathon event, the radler provides the ideal balance.

“It’s fine to be drunk [at Oktoberfest].” explains Dominic Blum, an engineer who spent five years working at a biergarten in Hanau, Germany that hosts a popular Oktoberfest event for Frankfurters who can’t make it down to Munich. “It’s not the best, but it’s normal. People misbehave and it’s expected. There’s always security around, and that’s why the glass mugs are so thick,” Blum adds.

The security isn’t meant to seem menacing or threatening though, but rather to allow people to freely drink without worry. This is also why radlers are always available as an option — so you don’t have to stop drinking.

Though the concept of this traditional beverage holds strong, the format continues to evolve. According to Blum, some now opt to mix their beer with sparkling water rather than lemon soda, optimizing hydration and preserving more of the beer’s flavor.

As booze consumption continues to trend downward, sessionable, low-ABV drinks and practices like zebra striping seem to be gaining a cultural foothold. While there’s a new flavor of canned seltzer or a low-ABV RTD available every season, the humble radler has always been available for those of us hoping to drink a bit less without skipping the party or beer festival entirely.

How to Make a Radler at Home

If you care to try it at home, here’s the recipe for the radler served at Oktoberfest:

Ingredients

  • 12 ounce can of Sprite
  • 12 ounce bottle of Bavarian lager, (Paulaner, Hofbräu, and Spaten are the easiest to find in the U.S. but it’s rare to see their festbier which has a stronger, maltier flavor than the standard helles style)

Directions

  1. Pour and combine the two beverages equally in the largest beer glass that you own.

While this makes a fine radler, and brings back fond memories of days spent clinking liter-sized mugs, there are much better beer-soda cocktails possible. A radler made with wheat beer and lemonade is called a “Russenmass” and combining lager and cola is a “Diesel.” Here’s my personal favorite radler lately:

Ingredients

  • 8 ounces of “Festbier” from a local craft brewery, or any helles lager
  • 4 ounces of San Pellegrino sparkling citrus soda (Any citrus flavor works! The citrus Spindrift seltzers also go well with helles lager)

Directions

  • Pour the beer into a glass until it’s about two-thirds full, and fill the rest of the glass with the soda.

content:
There are boundless ways to personalize a Martini. There’s dry with a twist, dirty with an olive, savory Gibsons, quaffable 50/50s … the list of customizations goes on. But the most significant and divisive specification is the choice of spirit: gin or vodka.

Just as which category of spirit goes into your Martini is critical, the brand of liquor should likewise not be an afterthought. While the gin category offers more diversity in flavor that can suit different Martini variations, choosing the right brand for a vodka Martini is equally important. Despite the common misconception, vodka isn’t always completely neutral, and each liquid’s base ingredients and production methods can have a major impact on the flavor of your ’tini.

So, we tapped top bartenders from across the country to recommend a specific vodka for three different Martini variations: classic with a twist, dirty with olives, and a wild card of their choice. Here are the best vodkas for each Martini variation, according to 11 bartenders.

Atticus Basehore

Head bartender, Chambers, New York City

Classic Martini: This is a drink for someone who really loves vodka with some nuance, so I’m grabbing Barr Hill Vodka. Distilled from raw honey, it has all of the aromatics of the base material without any sweetness.

Dirty Martini: I want a little spiciness and some rich texture to hold up against the olive brine. I tend to go for Polish rye vodkas because of their robust character. Wodka Vodka is produced from rye coming from a single estate, and it retains some beautiful black pepper notes along with a really full body.

50/50 Martini: I think 50/50 Martinis are beautiful with vodka because, deep in my soul, I’m really just a vermouth drinker. So, compared to other Martini specs, this format really shows off the vermouth you are using, but that doesn’t mean you can skimp on the vodka. Axberg from Reisetbauer is truly a masterclass in precision and is perfect accomplice to a solid vermouth.

Charlie Szur

Head Bartender, Confidant and Frenzie, NYC

Classic Martini: Belvedere. It has a rich, creamy mouthfeel with a subtle floral sweetness, delivering an inviting experience both in texture and flavor.

Dirty Martini: I’m a big fan of introducing a touch of sweetness to balance the strong, salty overtone of the drink, and Tito’s is the best vodka for the job. Made from corn, Tito’s retains a bit of that earthy, honeyed sweetness, pairing well with olive brine and salt.

Perfect Martini: I love to use Haku Vodka, made from white rice, in a Perfect Martini, which features both sweet and dry vermouth. The more mineral-forward palate provides a rich, savory-yet-sweet profile that perfectly matches the sweet vermouth.

Alex Howard

Bar director and co-owner, Martha My Dear, Nashville

Classic Martini: I’d choose Ketel One. It has enough grain character to actually contribute to the drink’s texture while remaining clean enough for the vermouth and lemon oil to still read. It also has a slight peppery finish that makes the Martini taste crisp rather than just cold and diluted.

Dirty Martini: I actually would also pick Ketel One for a Dirty Martini for the same reasons. Its subtle spice keeps the drink lively against all of the brine’s salt, and its dry finish keeps the drink from coming across too soft or sweet.

Alpine Martini: “Weird” Martini variations usually incorporate additional complexity, so I shift my focus to the other ingredients in the drink besides the vodka. Because of this, I would choose something softer, such as Tito’s. Its corn base gives a sweeter, rounder impression that can take a back seat and let the other elements shine. I particularly enjoy an Alpine Martini made with Tito’s, dry vermouth, Génépy, and a dash of orange bitters.

Tiffany Wang

General manager, Ops, NYC

Classic Martini: My pick for a classic Martini is Supergay Vodka because it provides a smooth base that allows for a clean finish. There’s also a touch of vanilla that balances the overall cocktail.

Dirty Martini: I love Tito’s for a Dirty Martini because it provides a blank canvas with a slight, underlying sweetness that allows the olive brine to shine.

Gibson: Tommyrotter makes a great small-batch vodka that has a slight peppery finish, complementing the briny bite from a pickled onion.

Natasha Van Duser

Co-owner, beverage director, and general manager, Bateman’s, NYC

Classic Martini: I like to reach for Altamura Distilleries vodka, an Italian vodka made from 100 percent durum wheat, which gives it a creamy, umami depth that other vodkas don’t have. A classic Martini is all about letting the base spirit be the shining star, so utilizing a vodka with a layered flavor profile is a must.

Dirty Martini: I like to use a crisp, clean vodka that will pair well with the brine, so I typically reach for Deep Eddy Vodka which is made out in Austin, Texas. It’s a corn-based vodka that is distilled 10 times and filtered through charcoal four times, removing any harshness and making it a great base for a Dirty Martini.

Any Martini riff: I always grab Truman Vodka. It’s a silky vodka made out in Austria that really lends itself to playing well with various flavors. It works great in both savory and sweet Martini riffs, whether I use it as the base for a white cheddar infusion paired with a gherkin brine for a salty Dirty Martini riff or pair it with shochu and a hint of lychee for a spirit-forward Lychee Martini.

José Medina Camacho

Beverage director and co-founder, Adiõs, Birmingham, Ala.

Classic Martini: Haku Japanese Vodka. I prefer a 50/50 split with Dolin dry vermouth, saline, and orange bitters, stirred and served with a lemon twist. I enjoy clean, crisp cocktails that are perfect for either starting or ending an evening.

Dirty Martini: Stolichnaya. It’s an easy, reliable, and consistent choice for a classic dirty preparation.

Taqueria Martini: This recipe features St. George Green Chile Vodka, Casa Mariol Vermut Blanco, and San Marcos pickled pepper brine (specifically from the whole jalapeño cans). It should be stirred, not shaken, and garnished with pickled peppers and carrots. Spicy and savory cocktails are my favorites, and this particular drink pairs beautifully with fried or Southern comfort food.

Conor Bandall

Bar manager, The View, NYC

Classic Martini: I like Ketel One here because it’s clean and crisp without being completely neutral. There’s a subtle citrus character and enough grain presence to stand alongside the vermouth, while still giving you that beautifully clean vodka Martini profile.

Dirty Martini: Belvedere. For a Dirty Martini, I want a vodka with a little more body and structure. Belvedere’s rye base gives it a lovely texture and enough character to stand up to olive brine rather than disappearing behind it.

Sake Martini: Haku’s soft, rounded texture and subtle sweetness from its rice base pair beautifully with a dry sake. In place of dry vermouth, sake amplifies vodka’s character instead of masking it, keeping a crisp, elegant, recognisably Martini-esque drink. Finish it with an expressed lemon.

Jennava Walker

Bar manager, Midnight Rambler, Dallas

Classic Martini: Ketel One brings a softness to the Martini that allows the vermouth to shine while keeping the classic build crisp, clean and balanced.

Dirty Martini: Grey Goose complements our house-blended olive mix beautifully. The vodka still holds its own while allowing the savory, salty flavor of the olives to come through.

Espresso Martini: Because Weber Ranch is an agave-based vodka, it brings the essence of tequila while still working perfectly in an Espresso Martini. We’ve seen growing interest in tequila-based Espresso Martinis in Texas, so it’s also a fun way to introduce guests to an agave-based, Texas-made spirit.

Lucky Preksto

Bar director, Bufón, NYC

Classic Martini: Hans Reisetbauer makes eau de vie, which is fantastic. He also makes a vodka, Axberg, named for the town where you can find his distillery. Incredibly smooth on the palate with a pleasant snap at the finish, Axberg makes a slick 2:1 Martini with a couple dashes of Regan’s.

Dirty Martini: We use Fort Hamilton Fortress Vodka out of Brooklyn for our house Dirty Martini, the Dirty Bufón. It’s a little meatier than the Reisetbauer and it’s got great character.

Reverse Martini: If you want to drink a lot of Martinis, just make them upside down with a 2:1 ratio of vermouth to vodka. Ketel One works great in these low-ABV Martinis. Keep the bitters, serve with olives or a twist, or both!

Keith Larry

Bartender and co-founder, Bar Etienne, NYC

Classic Martini: I tend to prefer Altamura Distilleries Vodka. The ABV is slightly higher at 43 percent, so its overall structure and aroma are enhanced. It’s pretty citrusy, so it’s well complemented by a lemon twist.

Dirty Martini: I would have to choose Haku. It’s a rice-based vodka filtered through bamboo charcoal, and it pairs really well without being overpowered by the brine.

Espresso Martini: I’ll choose Grey Goose, as it has a very velvety character and adapts well to both sweetness and bitterness. I use it for an Espresso Martini riff with toasted pistachios and black sesame.

Carlo Splendorini

Beverage director, Bar Sprezzatura, San Francisco

Classic Martini: I prefer Grey Goose because the French wheat gives it a creamy texture that balances perfectly with Carpano Bianco vermouth and the oil from a lemon twist. The combination is absolutely perfect and gives it a silky mouthfeel like no other when stirred gently for 15 to 20 seconds.

Dirty Martini: I still prefer Grey Goose because the brine from Sicilian Castelvetrano olives is rich and savory, so it pairs even better with the creaminess of the wheat. In this case, my ideal proportion is 2 ounces of vodka to 1 ounce of brine.

Gibson: Now, every place has its own feeling. Let’s say I’m sitting at a great old-school steakhouse — I feel like having a shaken vodka Gibson, ice-cold, no vermouth, with a pickled onion, please. My favorite! Still Grey Goose, which is great for Martinis, in my humble opinion.

content:
Dank cellars are a gold mine for some drinkers. Rather than opening a bottle of wine — or, in some cases, a can of beer — right away, some hobbyists let their alcohol sit on racks for many years to develop complex flavors. And for Americans in particular, one of the most popular collectible beverages is bourbon.

Collecting bottles of the corn-based American whiskey became a common hobby during the so-called “bourbon boom” of the 21st century, but some of the most coveted bottles date back much earlier. And while the boost in sales has waned and the American whiskey category now faces an oversupply, the prices for allocated bourbons keep climbing higher.

This year’s most expensive bourbon, for example, sold for over $10,000 more than last year’s top seller. While the rest of the bourbon industry struggles in the face of low demand, the rising prices for highly allocated bottlings suggests the allure of collectible bourbon shows no signs of slowing down.

From pre-Prohibition whiskeys to special releases, here are the most expensive bourbons in the world right now, according to Wine Searcher.

10. A.H. Hirsch Reserve 17 Year Old Straight Bourbon Whiskey, Pennsylvania, USA

A.H. Hirsch Reserve 17 comes from a historic line of whiskies. In 1974, Adolph Hirsch commissioned a 400-barrel batch of whiskey from a distillery in Schaefferstown, Penn. The whiskies aged untouched for 15 years, until the distillery ceased production in 1989 amid a slump in American whiskey consumption. Hirsch then moved the barrels to Kentucky, where they finished aging and were eventually bottled at 17 years old. The historic lore, coupled with the storied quality of the whiskey, resulted in some of the most coveted bottles of bourbon to date.

  • Average price: $28,801
  • ABV: 47.8%
  • Tasting notes: Toffee, oak, rye spice

9. Old Rip Van Winkle Selection 17 Year Old Pot Stilled Straight Bourbon Whiskey, Kentucky, USA

Casked in 1974 and bottled in 1991 by Julian Van Winkle III, this rare pot stilled Old Rip Van Winkle expression is believed to have been produced at the historic Old Boone Distillery. Originally intended for the Japanese market, this impressive 17-year-old bottling was later released in limited quantities as part of the sought-after Pappy Van Winkle Family Reserve line.

  • Average price: $29,086
  • ABV: 47.8%
  • Tasting notes: Vanilla, dried fruit, aged oak

8. Old Stagg 19 Year Old Straight Bourbon Whiskey, Kentucky, USA

This bourbon from the original George T. Stagg Distillery — now Buffalo Trace — in Frankfort, Ky. was distilled in 1914 and bottled in 1933 as a medicinal whiskey, a unique time capsule of how some distilleries continued production during Prohibition. Buffalo Trace has since revived the Old Stagg label as part of its Prohibition Collection.

  • Average price: $31,746
  • ABV: 50%
  • Tasting notes: Oak funk, rye spice, citrus zest

7. Redemption 36 Year Old Barrel Proof Straight Bourbon Whiskey, USA

Redemption debuted this high-age-statement bourbon as part of its lineup called “The Ancients” in 2017. With just 18 bottles released to the market, this 36-year-old, cask-strength bourbon is one of the most exclusive bottlings out there.

  • Average price: $35,999
  • ABV: 48.8%
  • Tasting notes: Dried citrus, baking spices, smoke

6. Old Rip Van Winkle ‘Van Winkle Special Reserve’ Corti Brothers 19 Year Old Straight Bourbon Whiskey, Kentucky, USA

Produced at the historic Stitzel-Weller Distillery in 1975, this wheated bourbon was distilled specifically for Corti Brothers, a legendary grocery store in Sacramento. When it came time to bottle the whiskey in 1994, Darrell Corti convinced Van Winkle III to package it in a cognac-style decanter.

  • Average price: $35,000
  • ABV: 45.7%
  • Tasting notes: Peach skin, toffee, pepper

5. Old Rip Van Winkle ‘Blue Smoke’ 18 Year Old Kentucky Straight Bourbon Whiskey, Kentucky, USA

Van Winkle III produced this ‘Blue Smoke’ bottling exclusively for Danny Meyer’s New York City barbecue restaurant of the same name in 2003. The origin of this whiskey has never been confirmed, though most collectors and inspectors speculate it came from Stitzel-Weller.

  • Average price: $45,998
  • ABV: 46.3%
  • Tasting notes: Espresso, toasted nuts, oak

4. Old Rip Van Winkle 25 Year Old Kentucky Straight Bourbon Whiskey, Kentucky, USA

Production of this coveted wheated bourbon began in 1989 at the now closed Van Winkle family distillery in Shively, Ky., before Sazerac relocated it to Buffalo Trace in 2002. After 25 years in barrel, the whiskey finished its maturation in stainless steel for three years before bottling. Only 710 bottles of this expression were released.

  • Average price: $46,428
  • ABV: 50%
  • Tasting notes: Oak, dark fruit, chocolate

3. Old Rip Van Winkle ‘Twisted Spoke’ 16 Year Old Kentucky Straight Bourbon Whiskey, Kentucky, USA

The label for Old Rip Van Winkle’s ‘Twisted Spoke’ expression is unlike any other in its lineup. Van Winkle III bottled this whiskey in 1999 for the notorious biker-themed Chicago bar of the same name, which closed in 2025.

  • Average price: $43,628
  • ABV: 52.5%
  • Tasting notes: Oak, cinnamon, cherry, vanilla

2. Old Rip Van Winkle Bottled in Bond Kentucky Straight Bourbon Whiskey, USA

This is an ultra-rare expression of Old Rip Van Winkle’s bottled-in-bond expression produced in 1916 and released in 1934. At the time, the label’s whiskeys were produced in Kentucky before they were aged in a Missouri warehouse and bottled in pint-sized decanters.

  • Average price: $57,301
  • ABV: 50%
  • Tasting notes: Caramel, vanilla, dark fruit

1. Society of Bourbon Connoisseurs 20 Year Old Cask Proof Bourbon Whiskey, Kentucky, USA

If you thought the most expensive bourbon had nothing to do with the Van Winkle name, think again. There is no Society of Bourbon Connoisseurs — Van Winkle III created the lofty title specifically for this label of 20-year-old cask strength bourbons he produced for the Japanese market.

  • Average price: $64,356
  • ABV: 53.5%
  • Tasting notes: Molasses, toffee, nuts, dried fruit

For others, it’s the last bastion of glee before a frustrating loss. Win or lose, though, the tailgate’s bevy of food and beverage enjoyed in revelry among good friends never ceases to delight. There is only one real rule to a tailgate: Have a good time.

content:
Tailgating is a traditional game day staple for many. It’s also the one moment of guaranteed Sunday afternoon happiness. For some football fans, it represents the initial spark of joy that gradually transforms into the afterglow of their favorite team’s triumph. For others, it’s the last bastion of glee before a frustrating loss. Win or lose, though, the tailgate’s bevy of food and beverage enjoyed in revelry among good friends never ceases to delight.

There is only one real rule to a tailgate: Have a good time. This simple mandate leaves what one chooses for their tailgating drink of choice to be completely open to interpretation. It may be something as basic as a crisp beer or as fancy as a pinkies-out cocktail. As long as the imbiber acts responsible, there are no wrong answers.

For bartenders, a Sunday tailgate can be a great way to unwind after back-to-back Friday and Saturday nights. It may take some effort to get out of the house, but the opportunity to be immersed in the unique social culture of the NFL tailgate with their beverage of choice makes overcoming the struggle worthwhile. With that in mind, we asked 15 bartenders about the one drink they tend to reach for most often when they tailgate prior to kickoff. In quite a few cases, supporting the local pro team also means throwing their support behind local products.

The go-to tailgating drinks for bartenders:

  • Miller Lite & Jameson Irish Whiskey
  • Rainier Beer
  • Monday Night Brewing 404 Lager and ASW Fiddler Wheated Bourbon
  • Michelada
  • Bloody Mary
  • Spicy Ranch Water
  • Huss Brewing Co. Devil’s Halo Lager
  • Freezer Door Old Fashioned
  • Sierra Nevada Pale Ale
  • Georgia Peach Mule
  • Suntory Toki Whisky Highball
  • Second District Brewing Co. Bancroft Beer and shot of Old Grand-Dad Bottled in Bond
  • Labatt Blue Light
  • Bubbly
  • Dibon Cava
  • Ranch Water
  • High Noon
  • Red Snapper

“Football calls for beer and whiskey, and when you have tickets to an NFL game and a tailgating opportunity, it’s a perfect pairing. However, It is important to consider the amount of time you will be consuming drinks, so you want to have a long-term plan. I personally like to stick to a lower ABV beer that is crisp and light if I plan to drink the whole day, and Miller Lite is perfect for the job. It also tastes delicious straight from a can, the preferred packaging in a parking lot. It can get really cold here in Chicago, and on these occasions, you need to supplement your beverage choice with something that will warm you up, like whiskey. My personal favorite is Jameson Irish Whiskey. It is straightforward, has a kick to remind you that you’re drinking whiskey, and warms you from the inside.” —Sarah Clark, director of operations and beverage director, The Dearborn, Chicago

“My go-to tailgating drink is Rainier Beer. As a transplant who’s called Seattle home for the past 12 years, Rainier has become the perfect bridge between where I came from and where I am now. I still miss cracking open a Yuengling back East and the nostalgia of PBR and Camel Lights outside my favorite dive bar, but Rainier has earned its place in the cooler on game day. It’s approachable, unpretentious, and deeply tied to the Pacific Northwest. Whether I’m watching my favorite NFL team or gathering with friends before kickoff, Rainier is the beer I reach for every time.” —Emelio Sansone, executive chef, Tin Lizzie Lounge, Seattle

“We love our Sundays and a full day of football, but when it comes to camaraderie and pride, nothing beats Monday Night Football. One game, one party, all eyes on the same ball. For that, only local beverages will do. There are two local Atlanta companies which reflect the hard work and passion that flow throughout the city: Fiddler Wheated Bourbon and 404 Lager from Monday Night Brewing. Fiddler has a rich history and delivers a spicy finish, and if you see me with an ice-cold 404, you’ll likely find me wearing a subtle smile and feeling perfectly content.” —William Cutting, F&B specialist, Hartley Kitchen and Cocktails, Atlanta

“I love tailgating. I’m not a sports guy though, so to me tailgating is reminiscent of a more chaotic brunch. This means it’s perfect for morning beverages, so I will want a spicy Michelada or Bloody Mary. If you’re going to support a local team, you need to also support local brands, so I’m using Threes Brewing Echo of Nothing for my Michelada. For my Bloody Mary, I’m using Sinpatch vodka by Tenmile Distilling.” —Atticus Bashore, head bartender, Chambers, New York City

“It’s Texas, so of course tailgaters want a Ranch Water. As football season arrives in Houston, fans are searching for a refreshing, palate-pleasing libation, and a Ranch Water — specifically, a Spicy Ranch Water — is an easy, build-on-the-spot cocktail anyone can make. With minimal prep — all you need to do is just pre-slice jalapeños and juice fresh lime — tailgaters can stay focused on the BBQ. The jalapeño adds subtle spice without reading as heavy throughout the day. Non-tequila drinkers can omit the tequila for a spirit-free version, providing three crowd-pleasing options to cheer on the Texans.” —Andrea Johns, bar lead, The Naturalist Bar & Lounge, Houston

“In 2024, Huss Brewing Co. announced a partnership with ASU (Arizona State University) to brew Devil’s Halo Lager, the official craft beer of Sun Devils Athletics. Each sale will benefit the Sun Angel Collective, which helps fund and broker Name, Image, and Likeness (NIL) deals for ASU student athletes. On Sundays, we’re drinking Devil’s Halo while we’re watching the Cardinals, but we are supporting our local University while also championing those who are trying to reach the ultimate stage in football.” —Ashley Traynor, F&B operations manager, The Phonecian Tavern, Scottsdale, Ariz.

“On those cold fall and winter mornings when you can barely feel your fingers, you need something a little stronger than a beer to keep you warm. What I like to drink in those situations is a freezer door Old Fashioned. You batch the cocktail at home with the bourbon, bitters, and syrup, then add water for dilution. No need to stir or bring any tools to the tailgate. Just pour, enjoy, and root for your team!” —Nick Kanakaris, general manager and beverage director, Aubrey’s Corner, Summit, N.J.

“My go-to tailgating drink would be Sierra Nevada Pale Ale. My husband is a huge football fan, and my first real experience watching football with him involved a Sierra Nevada Pale Ale, so the two have been connected in my mind ever since. It’s also become one of my go-to outdoorsy beers. I spend so much of my professional life thinking about wine — quality, flavor profiles, pairings, etc. — that sometimes it’s nice to just open a beer and enjoy it without analyzing anything. And Sierra Nevada’s bitterness is exactly what I want, especially with jalapeño poppers.” —Kinga Mackowiak, beverage director, Apple Blossom, Denver

“My go-to tailgating drink is a Georgia Peach Mule, made with bourbon, spicy roasted peach purée, fresh muddled lime, agave nectar, and Fever-Tree Ginger Beer. It has everything I want for game day: It’s cold and refreshing, with some heat from the roasted peaches and just enough sweetness to balance the bourbon and lime. It also feels distinctly Georgian without becoming overly complicated. The ingredients can be batched ahead of time, then topped with ginger beer when everyone is ready for a drink, so it’s easy to serve to a group without spending the entire tailgate mixing cocktails.” —Damien McGee, owner, Vesper, Atlanta

“Our go-to tailgating drink would be a Suntory Toki Japanese Whisky Highball. For tailgating, I like something refreshing, simple, and easy to enjoy with food, and a Toki Highball checks all of those boxes. The whisky’s light, crisp character with plenty of cold soda makes it refreshing without overpowering the food, especially grilled meats and barbecue. It’s also easy to make and serve, which is exactly what you want when you’re tailgating.” —Tana Kokanot, head bartender, Jeong Yuk Jeom, NYC

“In South Philly, there are few things we love more than a Citywide Special: Philadelphia’s pairing of an affordable beer and a shot of whiskey. Whether you’re watching from your favorite bar or in the Birds’ parking lot, for me, a pint of Bancroft Beer from Second District Brewing alongside a shot of Old Grand-Dad Bottled in Bond always kicks off an Eagles game in good fashion. Go Birds!” —Chris Liu, beverage director, Bloomsday, Philadelphia

“Living in the city of Buffalo and being a Bills fan, I have grown up drinking Labatt Blue Light at almost every tailgate I have ever been to. It’s crisp, classic, reliable, and low ABV enough that you will become full before you’ve drunk enough to make a complete fool of yourself. Another beautiful thing about football is the 1 p.m. Sunday start time, which means arriving at the stadium before 9 a.m. If you are starting that early, the only alternative to beer to drink that early in the morning is bubbly. Prosecco or Cava made into something fun and delicious; preferably a spritz with a little soda water to keep it lower in alcohol content. My favorite Cava right now is Dibon — it’s super delicious and high quality for the price point and makes a phenomenal spritz.” —Mary Bennett, bar manager, Mira, Buffalo

“My vote is a Ranch Water: grab a Topo Chico in a glass bottle, open it, drink some, then add a quality blanco tequila and a slice of lime. I’ve been digging the Cascahuín Tahona Blanco. The great thing about this method is that you control your own ratio as the day goes on, and if you want to skip a few rounds, no one notices. It’s built for a day full of tailgating.” —Justin Ware, operations director, Johnny’s Gold Brick, Houston

“My go-to tailgate drink is a High Noon. I’m definitely a seltzer girly, especially on game day, because I want something light and refreshing that won’t leave me feeling weighed down. Tailgating in Detroit can easily become an all day event, so I like something I can sip while comfortably pacing myself while cheering on the Lions.” —Tara Wong, beverage manager, Gilly’s Clubhouse, Detroit

“I love a Red Snapper made with Dorothy Parker New York Gin for tailgating (and pretty much any other Sunday occasion). The gentle fruit and florality of the gin pair really nicely with the spice and acidity of the tomato, citrus, Worcestershire, and hot sauce, making it particularly sessionable. Add a celery stick, an olive, and, if you’re peckish, a cooked shrimp, and you’re set for game day.” —Jamie Gordon, bar and creative director, Jaywalker, NYC

title: A Restaurant’s Off-Menu Wine List Should Feel Special, Not Exclusive
summary:
When I travel, I tend to go a bit extreme in my research of where I should eat and drink. Years ago, before taking a trip to Amsterdam, it was no different. During my weeks of research, I stumbled upon a new spot whose Instagram feed was chock full of wine nerd clickbait, but one post in particular caught my eye: “These Gems are Hiding in Our Wine Room: Kenjiro Kagami’s Domaine des Miroirs.” Naturally, I wanted to raid that wine room.

content:
When I travel, I tend to go a bit extreme in my research of where I should eat and drink. Years ago, before taking a trip to Amsterdam, it was no different. During my weeks of research, I stumbled upon a new spot whose Instagram feed was chock full of wine nerd clickbait, but one post in particular caught my eye: “These Gems are Hiding in Our Wine Room: Kenjiro Kagami’s Domaine des Miroirs.” Naturally, I wanted to raid that wine room.

We arrived at the restaurant and cafe, and I dug through the list only to find it was not there. I assumed someone had the same idea I had, came in, and bought it. I could find another wine, but I had to ask. What followed was my first true experience with the “off list” wine. It was an interrogation, albeit a very kind and hospitable one.

“How do you know this wine?”

“What do you know about this wine and its winemaker?”

“Have you ever had this wine before?”

“Are there other producers from this region that you really love?”

“What other wines are you really into right now?”

“Are there other wines that you see on the list that interest you?”

Some of these questions were things a somm may ask a guest when trying to figure out what wines to suggest, but this was different. It was a test, a very polite test, but a test all the same. Ultimately, I passed, after which it was explained, apologetically, that the restaurant only received a few bottles a year and they wanted to make sure each went to someone who would appreciate it.

The wine was great, the meal was great, and the service was solid. Overall, it was a great meal, though, to be honest, it did strike me as a bit odd and a little off-putting in the beginning. While this wine was definitely culty and nerdy at that time, it had yet to reach the unicorn status it has now. They did post the wine publicly, and that alone would attract people who appreciate it. It was most likely meant to bring in wine lovers like myself to the space, so why gatekeep it?

I’d mostly forgotten about this experience until a friend told me about something similar that had recently happened to him in Manhattan.

He went to a well known restaurant, and one of the servers recognized him immediately as a wine professional and let him know they had some amazing “off list” wines. He ordered one of the wines and loved it. He went back a few weeks later and inquired about the wine, but this time he had a different server.

“That wine isn’t on the list. Where did you have it?”

“Here.”

“Who served it to you?”

“Another server, I don’t remember his name.”

“Here?”

“Yes, here.”

After a pause, there was a, “Yeah, we have it.”

Mind you, this was not a unicorn $500 bottle with only two cases imported to the United States. It was a sub $100 wine from an unsung appellation. Needless to say, it left a bit of a bad taste in my friend’s mouth.

I was amazed by the absurdity and frustration of it, but the story brought me back to Amsterdam. What would my experience have been if I hadn’t answered the questions correctly? Would they have denied me? How would I have felt? Would I have been embarrassed? One thing is certain: I would not have felt better about myself or my experience at the restaurant, and I’m guessing others would not feel great about it either.

I want to lay this out from a hospitality perspective. I’m of the school that everyone should get a wonderful and equitable experience at a restaurant or bar, and that everyone should feel like they are getting something special. Having a separate list just for regulars and wine nerds goes against that.

Daniel Eddy of Brooklyn’s celebrated Winner and Runner Up has long talked about having a separate list, though he doesn’t view the potential list as a secret. He looks at it in a similar way to a rewards program punch card. If a guest dines with them five or 10 times, they would “unlock” a special list with rare, allocated bottles at a fair, nongouged price. He sees the possibility as more of a known reward for consistent patronage.

His reasoning is that he has a pretty deep list of special, hard to get wines at below market prices. Some are his personal consignments. When he first opened, there were several guests who would come in, cherry pick all the special wines, and never come back again. “I’d rather reward those who become regulars than let the cherry-pickers clean out the list and never return,” he says. As of today, he has not implemented this strategy but hopes to someday soon.

I get it. Wine directors don’t get many bottles of certain wines, and they want them to go to people who will both enjoy and appreciate them. You also want your regulars to feel special, but I don’t love the practice. How do you handle the guest who asks for the “secret list,” but isn’t a regular or someone you know? They clearly know about the list. They’re asking. How can you be hospitable in that situation?

I know of a restaurant where somms are instructed to tell guests a listed bottle is 86’d if the wine director doesn’t know the guest or thinks they don’t “deserve” the wine. It’s crazy to me that this happens, but sadly it does, and this type of gatekeeping is exactly why wine is struggling these days.

If you list a wine, everyone should be able to buy it, regardless of their knowledge of wine. Most guests who come in aren’t going to know as much as the somm, and yes, the somm can and should try to steer people toward wines they think the guest will love and away from wines they may not enjoy as much. But if the guest sees something on the list and wants to pay for it, it should not be withheld. It’s bad business among other things.

None of this is without caveats. I would be lying if I said I never sold off-list wines. I have. At my restaurant LaLou, we had plenty of wines that were not listed for a variety of reasons.

Some wines needed time and were purposely held in the cellar until we thought they were ready to go. Occasionally, someone would come in and want that particular style of wine. We might sell them a bottle with the understanding that “it might be a bit tight” or “it’s a bit young, but let’s see where it’s at.”

Some wine lists only have a limited amount of space, and some places will keep wines off because they simply don’t have room and are waiting for another wine to run out before they can print it. I would 100 percent sell that wine off-list to a guest who was looking for something similar. Sometimes I would sell wines that had just arrived and we had not had time to list them, but I would sell the wine based on the guest’s preferences, not on who the guest was or what they did or didn’t know about the wine.

It’s important to note that these wines were not on a separate “cool kids,” industry or regulars list. They were offered to any guests who were not finding what they wanted on our list, and we were attempting to give them a special experience. It wasn’t a strategic “special list” for certain guests. It was happenstance that allowed us to do this, and I think that is the main point.

Here, it’s the intent that counts. Hospitality is giving people something they didn’t know they wanted. A special list for the worthy or those in the know is antithetical to that. It doesn’t create new regulars, it rewards the current ones while running the risk of alienating potential ones.

At a moment when we are barraged with stories that hospitality is at a breaking point and wine consumption is at a breaking point, that restaurants are going out of business, and grape growers are ripping out vines, we should be thinking of ways to get more people in the doors and drinking more wine, not excluding guests and potential wine drinkers.

content:
From the boozy and caffeinated Espresso Martini to the provocative, passion fruit-spiked Pornstar Martini, many of the bar world’s most beloved modern classics were invented in London. But beyond these household names there’s another London-born cocktail that’s been largely flying under the radar — though it might be ready for its main character moment.

The East 8 Hold-Up, a humble combination of vodka, Aperol, lime juice, pineapple juice, simple syrup, and passion fruit syrup, recently ranked No. 45 on Drinks International’s annual list of the most popular cocktails in the world. Sandwiched between beloved, well-known concoctions like the Piña Colada and the Vieux Carré, its inclusion on the list might seem to have come out of left-field. But the cocktail is far from new. Created in 2010, the East 8 Hold-Up has been quietly gaining steam over the years, likely winning over fans with its approachable flavor profile, recognizable ingredients, and bright color.

Bartender Kevin Armstrong first mixed up the drink at Milk & Honey’s London location. Londoners and others familiar with the city probably understand the connotations that the “East 8,” colloquially known as E8, neighborhood holds: At the time, it was a rough-around-the-edges area of the city, riddled with robberies and other crime.

In 2010, Armstrong was brainstorming ways to create new and exciting spins on cocktails served in a traditional format. During the first eight years of the bar’s run, most of its menus featured classic cocktails without much innovation, Armstrong told the magazine “Australian Bartender” in a 2010 interview. When it was his turn to write the menu, he wanted to add a new, modern vodka cocktail that followed a similar format to old-school drinks.

During that time, Armstrong and fellow bartender Sam Jeveons were venturing home after a night out together. Armstrong, who’d lived in East 8 at the time, had just parted ways with Jeveons when the latter stopped to, well, “take a leak.” While relieving himself with his pants around his ankles, a man approached him from behind, stepped on his pants, and demanded his wallet.

As Armstrong tells it: Rather than letting the robber get away with his wallet, Jeveons chased the thief around East 8 with his pants down to his ankles. The bit became known as the East 8 Hold-Up between the two of them.

Though the event itself has little to do with the build of the cocktail, the incident provided a catchy name for Armstrong’s vodka-based creation. The drink combines vodka, Aperol, pineapple and lime juices, and simple and passion fruit syrups, shaken until it develops a frothy texture. The bright orange concoction — which gets its color from the combination of Aperol and passion fruit — is poured over ice in a rocks glass, garnished with a duo of pineapple and lime wedges. The cocktail is tangy and fruity — but not overwhelmingly so, as the heft of the vodka and bitterness of Aperol balance out the syrups and juices.

According to Drinks International, the East 8 Hold-Up has gained traction among contemporary drinks savants worldwide. While not quite a household name yet, the drink can be found on an increasing number of craft cocktail menus. Bars like Satan’s Whiskers and Café Clement in London offer the drink, but the East 8 Hold-Up also crossed the pond and landed on the menu at Beef & Liberty Bar, the cocktail haunt above Hawksmoor’s Chicago location.

The East 8 Hold-Up isn’t the only British beverage that’s recently gained traction in international markets, especially in the U.S. The Gimlet, which was famously invented for the British Royal Navy, is enjoying a heyday among a certain set of drinkers. And one of New York City’s hottest newcomers, Dean’s, serves oysters over a shot of Guinness, a time-tested pub classic. What’s next for the “British Invasion” in stateside bars and restaurants? Expect the East 8 Hold-Up to round the corner.

Glenmorangie is joining the wave of ultra-aged whiskey releases. On Thursday, the Highland distillery announced the launch of a 50-year-old single malt, marking the distillery’s oldest Scotch yet.

The half century-old whisky is one of the final Glenmorangie expressions to come from barley malted on site, a process that the distillery ceased in 1977. The special release is the result of the vision of Glenmorangie’s director of distilling Dr. Bill Lumsden, who oversaw the Scotch’s maturation for its last 30 years. After joining the team in 1995, Lumsden identified a number of casks with potential for long term aging. In 1999, Lumsden brought together a small selection of bourbon cask- and sherry butt-aged whiskies for the project, and left the marriage to rest in a hogshead barrel for another 27 years.

Glenmorangie 50 Years Old was non-chill filtered and bottled at 45.7 percent ABV (91.4 proof). Brand tasting notes highlight baking spices, toffee, and leather on the nose. The palate brings pepper, tea leaves, grape must, and oak tannin, leading into a long, spice-forward finish.

The distillery commissioned renowned ceramicists Peter and Laurie Pincus to create the sleek porcelain package design. The pair developed an elegant, oval-shaped vessel that features 50 different colors as a nod to the whisky’s age.

The exceedingly exclusive bottling — only 149 numbered bottles of Glenmorangie 50 Years Old exist — hit the market for a suggested retail price of £25,800 ($36,000). It is available to select retailers, through Moët Hennessy Private Client Team network, and at the distillery’s visitor center in Tain, Scotland.

content:
Chardonnay is one of the world’s most popular grape varieties, but not every bottle is created equally. With the grape’s wide range of expressions and price points, it can sometimes seem difficult to find the middle ground between the ultra-rich, overly oaky budget bottles and the more nuanced, terroir-driven wines with daunting price tags.

But you don’t have to spend a fortune to explore all that Chardonnay has to offer beyond the notorious butter bombs that once gave the grape a bad name. To help pinpoint which bottles deliver the ample quality without the sticker shock that can come with high-end Chardonnay, we asked nine sommeliers from across the country which bottles they think offer the most bang for your buck. From surprisingly affordable White Burgundy to complex Chardonnays from buzzy Oregon producers, here are their picks for the best value Chardonnays.

The best bang-for-your-buck Chardonnays, according to sommeliers:

  • Lioco Sonoma Coast Chardonnay
  • On Wine Hill “Millerandage” Chardonnay 2024
  • Brij Wines Chardonnay
  • Enfield Wine Co. Citrine Chardonnay
  • Enfield Wine Co. Brosseau Chardonnay
  • Evening Land Vineyards Seven Springs Chardonnay
  • Lingua Franca Avni Chardonnay 2024
  • Scar of the Sea SLO Coast Chardonnay 2024
  • Domaine des Terres de Chatenay Mâcon-Villages “La Cuvée de Béracius” 2025

“I’m quite fond of the Lioco Sonoma Coast Chardonnay. It’s an unoaked style that tends to show bright acidity and some Chablis-like qualities. Generally, you can get it for around $25 retail, and it’s from a small, family-run winery.” —Gregory Wilson, sommelier, Beckon, Denver

“When it comes to delicious and affordable Chardonnay, so much great wine is being made on the West Coast right now. One of my favorites that has caught my attention lately is the On Wine Hill “Millerandage” Chardonnay 2024 from the Willamette Valley, Ore. Jeff Vejr is doing some really cool things in Oregon, and for this particular wine, he is using a specific clone (548) of Chardonnay that is predisposed to what is known as ‘millerandage’ or ‘hens and chicks.’ This causes uneven ripening of the grape clusters so some berries will be larger while others remain small. This increases the skin-to-juice ratio, giving the wine a beautiful, finely grained texture, as well as a natural kick of acidity from the tart, smaller berries in the bunch. This wine has the textural richness to hold up to a variety of foods, but it’s also fresh and fun enough to be enjoyed on its own!” —Cameron Dellinger, wine director, Jungsik, New York City

“I would love to shout out the Chardonnay from Brij Wines from the San Luis Obispo Coast. This project, from renowned California winemaker and master sommelier Raj Parr, uses fruit purchased from local growers who share his passion for sustainable farming. The winemaking is as thoughtful and non-interventionist as you find in any of the bottlings at Parr Wines but at a fraction of the price, typically retailing around $35. The wine itself has the rich texture and subtle oak aromas that I’m looking for in a California Chardonnay, but with salinity and freshness that speak to the wine’s coastal origins.” —Audrey Dowling, beverage director, Rye Bunny, Washington, D.C.

“I’ve always had a soft spot in my heart for the wines of Enfield Wine Company and found they’ve always delivered far beyond its price point. Winemaker John Lockwood comes from the pedigree of Littorai and Failla, two wineries that I would define as American winemaking excellence, as well as a commitment to working with small farmers in select California heritage sites that stand out to him. At $30 retail, the Citrine is far from the traditional California Chardonnay that has left a bad taste in the mouth of many wine drinkers, but offers a soft touch of yellow apple and citrus with a round tropical finish bursting with a kiss of saline minerality. Just writing about the wine makes me want to open another bottle from Enfield sooner than later.” —Angel Prado, lead sommelier, Sorelle, Charleston

“I love the Enfield Wine Co. Brosseau Chardonnay. It’s planted on super high elevation, limestone soils in Chalone, giving it this really distinct California terroir. There’s lean, mineral, acidity but it finishes lush, savory, round, and complex. It’s a great wine to get you from start to finish in the meal. The winemakers are really excited to be sharing the unique terroirs of California while celebrating dedicated farmers and growers in the region.” —Charlotte Mirzoeff, general manager and beverage director, Arthur, Brooklyn

“I think Evening Land Vineyards Chardonnay ‘Seven Springs’ from Eola Amity Hills, Ore. is the best affordable Chardonnay. At around $29 retail, this wine is as close to Meursault as you can find in the U.S. and at a fraction of the cost. It’s slightly reductive, just ripe enough and loaded with the savory mineral notes that are the backbone of all great Chardonnays.” —Francesco Grosso, wine director, Ai Fiori, NYC

“The current belief that the best place outside Burgundy to grow Chardonnay is the Willamette Valley, Ore. I have consistently been pleased with the Burgundian character of Chardonnays from Willamette Valley. My favorite is Lingua Franca Avni Chardonnay 2024, made by cherished Burgundy winemaker Dominique Lafon and Master Sommelier Larry Stone, with protégé Thomas Savre. It tastes like dipping your toe in a Meursault.” —Lindsey Geddes, wine director, Carversteak, Las Vegas

“With Scar of the Sea SLO Coast Chardonnay, you’re getting a bright and fresh expression of coastal California Chardonnay, with a long élevage and incredible farming practices. It has energy and depth, and punches way above its price point!” —Shanna Nasiri, owner, With Others, Brooklyn

“Domaine des Terres de Chatenay Mâcon-Villages ‘La Cuvée de Béracius’ 2025. I’m always excited to find a White Burgundy that overdelivers, and this old-vine Mâcon-Villages from Jean-Claude and Marie-Odile Janin is one I keep coming back to. Made from 70-year-old Chardonnay vines planted in the clay-limestone soils of Péronne, it has vibrant fruit, chalky minerality, and incredible tension. It has the focus and depth I love in great Burgundy while still feeling fresh and distinctive, so much so that we carry it at Le Pavillon. This limited-production cuvée is that rarest of finds: a true ‘unicorn’ wine from the Mâconnais.” —John Osborne, head sommelier, Le Pavillon, NYC

content:
This article is part of our Cocktail Chatter series, where we dive into the wild, weird, and wondrous corners of history to share over a cocktail and impress your friends.

The French baguette is losing steam: From 1970 to 2022, the number of traditional boulangeries in France dropped by roughly 400 a year from about 55,000 to 35,000. In response, the United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization (UNESCO) granted the French baguette its Intangible Cultural Heritage designation to preserve the tradition of breadmaking.

Though the numbers might suggest this culinary staple is waning, there still appears to be no shortage of baguettes in the country. In Paris, pedestrians will see locals and tourists alike walking the streets with the loaf of bread in tow, either clutched under the arm or poking out of a bag. The city also hosts a prestigious annual competition to find the best baguette in Paris, in which over 100 bakers submit their best loaves to be measured, weighed, and tasted for a chance to win a cash prize and a one-year contract to be the exclusive baguette supplier to the French president’s residence. But for those looking to experience the country’s carb culture in the most authentic way, there’s only one type of baguette to order.

The best baguettes slung around Paris are of a certain, government-controlled variety, thanks to a French law passed in 1993. The 1993 décret du pain (the bread decree), which sought to protect the sacred practice of breadmaking, legislated that baguettes labeled “tradition” must be made with just wheat flour, water, salt, and yeast or sourdough starter — no preservatives or other additives. The dough can also never be frozen, and the baguettes must be baked on the site where they are sold. “Baguettes de tradition” is the only government-controlled bread category.

The designation works much like the Appellation d’Origine Contrôlée (AOC) system, which mandates that wines labeled under a given region must follow specific quality and production standards, such as permitting certain grapes, aging methods, and additives. Similarly, at boulangeries around the country, loaves of bread are often placed into different baskets, with each label corresponding to the respective variety.

Ordering a stick from the tradition — aptly named and easy to remember, as it is the most traditional variety — basket ensures you’ll be eating the highest-quality bread, one with a craggly and sturdy exterior that opens to a bouncy, stretchy interior. Flavors of toasted and fresh yeast will be strong throughout.

Other baguette varieties include the “baguette classique” (also labeled as “ordinaire”) and the “baguette aux céréales” (also labeled as “aux graines”). A classique is a run-of-the-mill baguette, not protected under any government regulations, meaning the dough could have been frozen or it could contain preservatives to elongate its shelf life. A baguette aux céréales is the multigrain version of a baguette, with seeds and grains studding the loaf.

When ordering a baguette — whether de tradition or not — there are some other ways to communicate with the boulanger to ensure the bread will suit your specifications. Those who like sturdy, crunchy bread can ask for one bien cuite, or well cooked. Those who like a softer and more chewy loaf can ask for one pas trop cuite, or not too cooked. In either case, the baker will inspect their loaves and hand you the one that best suits your needs.

Whether mass-produced or not, any baguette in France is likely to be tasty and to evoke warm, happy feelings of European life. But when traveling the country, ordering your bread à la française can elevate that feeling, one yeasty crunch at a time.
